title: Methodus generalior numeros quosvis satis grandes perscrutandi utrum sint primi necne?

deep.reconstruction:
Context: E719 tests whether N = αa² + βb², with αβ an idoneal ('convenient') number, is prime. Euler's criterion is that N (coprime to αβ, in a primitive representation) is prime exactly when the representation is unique. To test this he looks for a second representation N = αx² + βy². This page treats α = 40, β = 13, so αβ = 520 = 8·5·13. The starting equation is 40a² − 13(y² − b²) = 40x², which is equivalent to 40(a² − x²) = 13(y² − b²).

End of §48 (carried over from p.29). In Case II (y+b = 20p, y−b = 2q), the differences of S = 13s(10s−b) grow by the constant 260. They are subtracted successively from a² while watching for a square.

§49, 'Alia evolutio'. Here b is odd, so for odd y the factor 8 in y² − b² is automatic. Set y = 2z ± b. Then y² − b² = 4z(z ± b), and dividing by 8 gives 5a² − (13/2)(z² ± bz) = 5x². The term z(z ± b) is always even, so the middle term is an integer. Five must divide z or z ± b. These cases are interchangeable by flipping the sign of b, so take z = 5s. Dividing by 5 gives a² − (13/2)(5s² ± bs) = x².

§50. Tabulate S(s) = (13/2)(5s² ± bs) for s = 0, ±1, ±2, …:
- S = 0, (13/2)(5 ± b), (13/2)(20 ± 2b), (13/2)(45 ± 3b), (13/2)(80 ± 4b).
- First differences: (13/2)(5 ± b), (13/2)(15 ± b), (13/2)(25 ± b), (13/2)(35 ± b).
- Second difference (p.31): (13/2)·10 = 65.
The procedure is a Fermat-style sieve: subtract cumulative differences from a² and check whether any remainder is a square.

§51. One substitution, y = 10s ± b, removes the whole factor 40 at once. Then y² − b² = 100s² ± 20bs, and dividing by 40 gives (13/2)(5s² ± bs) again. Euler generalises to α = 2^λ·f·g: put y = 2^{λ−1}fz ± b, so y² − b² = 2^{2λ−2}f²z² ± 2^λ bfz. Dividing by 2^λ f gives 2^{λ−2}fz² ± bz. Any remaining factors are to be removed by the general precepts given elsewhere.

§52, the 'simplest' evolution. Write the second representation as N = 40x² + 13y², so 13b² − 40(x² − a²) = 13y². Put x = 13s ± a and divide by 13: b² − 40(13s² ± 2as) = y². Now one subtracts S = 40(13s² ± 2as) from b². The table is on p.32: first differences 40(13 ± 2a), 40(39 ± 2a), …, with second difference 40·26 = 1040. Examples there: N = 85333, 89293, 99733 (all with b = 81).

Purpose: to organise the search for a second representation as cheaply as possible, by choosing the variable to sieve on so that the subtracted quadratic has the smallest growth. Here that means sieving on the a-variable with the smaller coefficient 13, so that b² is the large square.
errors: §50 table, third entry of the Difference column: the print reads (13/2)(45∓b) (the transcription marks it [?]). The correct value is S(3) − S(2) = (13/2)(45 ± 3b) − (13/2)(20 ± 2b) = (13/2)(25 ± b). This is a misprint: the constant growth of 65 stated on p.31 is consistent only with 25.
§50 table, last S entry: printed (13/2)(80+4b). It should be (13/2)(80 ± 4b), matching the other rows.

§51, general rule y = 2^{λ−1}fz ± b: as written it is more restrictive than the worked case. For α = 40 (λ = 3, f = 5) it gives y = 20z ± b, whereas Euler himself correctly uses y = 10s ± b just before. For odd y the factor 8 is automatic, so the modulus should be 2^{λ−2}f when λ = 3. In general the conditions y ≡ ±b mod 2^{λ−1} and y ≡ ±b mod f carry independent signs. A single '±' therefore misses the mixed-sign residue classes, e.g. α = 112 = 16·7 or 240. Read literally, the rule could miss a second representation and so wrongly certify a composite as prime. Euler hedges by deferring 'reliqui factores' to the general precepts.
Minor: in §49 the choice z = 5s 'perinde est' is justified by sign symmetry of b. This is correct only because both signs ± are carried through, which Euler does.

ideas.what: Primality test for N = αa² + βb² (αβ idoneal) by searching for a second representation; N is prime iff the representation is unique.
ideas.modern_name: Euler's idoneal (convenient) numbers primality criterion; one class per genus for discriminant −4αβ
ideas.where_published: E708, E715, E718, E719, E725 and related papers (Nova Acta / Opuscula analytica); discussed in Weil, Number Theory: an approach through history

ideas.what: Reducing the second-representation search to a² − S(s) = x² with S quadratic in s, scanned by subtracting first differences that grow by a constant second difference.
ideas.modern_name: Difference-table sieve, cf. Fermat's factorization method
ideas.usually_credited_to: Fermat (difference-of-squares method); Euler for this adaptation

ideas.what: Choosing the substitution (y = 10s ± b, or x = 13s ± a) by solving y² ≡ b² modulo the relevant factor, to remove the even part and a prime factor at once, and choosing the variable that gives the smallest search.
ideas.modern_name: Using residues of square roots mod m to restrict the search (CRT on square roots)

deep.surprise_reason: Routine worked case of Euler's well-studied idoneal-number primality method. The only noteworthy points are a printed misprint in the difference table and an over-restrictive general substitution in §51. Neither is a missed result.
transcription_corrections: §50 table, third Diff entry: the image shows (13/2)(45∓b), a print error for (13/2)(25±b). The transcription's '[?]' should be resolved this way, noting the misprint.
§50 table, s = ±4 row: the print shows (80+4b), which should be read as (80±4b).
§51: 'y = 10s ± b' and 'yy − bb = 100ss ± 20bs' are correctly transcribed although the scan is faint ('i(s', '1:c ss').
